sections.history: Tiruvandarkoil stands in the level country between Villupuram and Puducherry, and its Shiva temple is among the old shrines of the Nadu Nadu region sung in the Tevaram, which makes it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. The hymns of Tirugnana Sambandar, gathered in the First Thirumurai, praise the Lord here as Vadukeeswarar, also honoured as Panchanadeeswarar. Tradition reads the town's name from Vadukur, or Andar Koil, which in time became Tiruvandarkoil. The temple was raised in stone by the Cholas and carries inscriptions of the later Chola kings, among them Rajaraja Chola I and Kulottunga Chola I; today it stands as a protected monument in the care of the Archaeological Survey of India, worn but enduring.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east and is held within concentric rectangular walls of granite, a plain and ancient enclosure without the towering gopuram of the larger temples of the plains. The sanctum of Vadukeeswarar is reached through a mahamandapam and an arthamandapam, the pillared halls that lead the devotee inward by degrees. The goddess Tripurasundari is honoured in her own shrine within the second precinct. As a monument under the Archaeological Survey of India, the temple keeps the bare, unembellished dignity of a very old Chola foundation rather than the colour of a busy modern shrine.
sections.legends: The temple's story is told of the demon Mundasuran, who by hard-won boons grew able to torment Brahma and the gods. To end his reign Shiva commanded Vaduka Bhairava, one of the eight Bhairavas who guard the directions, to destroy him. The deed done, Vaduka Bhairava came to this place and worshipped the Lord to be freed of the sin that clings even to a righteous killing, and from his penance the Lord took the name Vadukeeswarar. For this reason the Bhairava is held in special regard here, and devotees keep his worship with particular care on Karthigai Ashtami.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri in the Tamil month of Masi, in February or March, is the temple's principal festival, kept as at every Shiva shrine with a night-long vigil and worship. Vaikasi Visakam in May or June and Skanda Sashti in the autumn are also observed, and special rites are offered to Bhairava on Karthigai Ashtami, in keeping with the temple's legend. As the festivals follow the Tamil calendar, confirm the dates locally before travelling.
sections.experience: Tiruvandarkoil rewards the devotee who seeks out the quiet of an old stone sanctuary. The temple sits a little apart from the busy Villupuram–Puducherry road, and within its granite walls the air is still. Come to the sanctum of Vadukeeswarar through the pillared halls, honour the goddess Tripurasundari in her shrine, and pause before the Bhairava, whose penance gave the temple its name. Being a protected monument, it is plainer than many living temples, and that plainness is part of its appeal for those who come in search of antiquity and calm.

visit.timings: Typically open for a few hours in the morning and again in the evening, with a long midday closure; as a smaller temple the hours can vary, so confirm locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. As this is a protected monument, ask the temple or site staff before photographing.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruvandarkoil lies on the Villupuram–Puducherry highway, about 21 km east of Villupuram and roughly 20 km west of Puducherry town. Both are served by frequent buses along the highway, and Villupuram is the nearest major railway junction; the temple stands close to the road at the village.
